summaries.example: Imagine two students. One writes an excellent report, and the other turns in almost no work. It may seem fair for the first student to deserve a high grade and the second to deserve a low grade. But suppose the school rules promise a refund for a broken science kit. A student may be entitled to that refund because a rule or promise says so, even if the student did nothing to deserve it. Desert and entitlement can point to the same result, but they are not the same idea.
summaries.summary: Desert is the idea that someone should receive something because of a feature, action, or condition connected with that person. A student may deserve a high grade because of excellent work. An athlete may deserve a prize because of outstanding performance. Someone harmed through no fault of their own may deserve help or compensation. These claims are different from entitlement. Entitlement depends on rules, laws, contracts, or other institutions. A customer may be entitled to a refund because of a guarantee, even if the refund is not based on the customer’s effort or character. A person may also deserve something without any rule promising it. The entry studies the parts of desert claims: who deserves, what is deserved, what the basis is, and sometimes who should provide it. It also asks how we can justify such claims. Philosophers have tested several ideas. Maybe giving people what they deserve produces good results, but useful results can sometimes come from giving someone something undeserved. Maybe institutions explain desert, but existing institutions can be unfair, and desert can arise where no institution exists. Ideas about approval, blame, responsibility, timing, and important values also help explain some cases, but none settles every question. The entry then considers whether desert affects what is valuable, including the value of a world in which people receive suitable levels of well-being. Finally, it examines theories saying that justice is mainly a matter of receiving what one deserves, while noting disagreements about whether desert can guide political and economic distribution.
key_ideas: Desert is not always the same as entitlement. A rule can give someone a right to something even when people think the person does not deserve it.
A desert claim usually has three parts: a deserver, a desert, and a desert base.
People can deserve good things, bad things, or ordinary things. A person might deserve a prize, a penalty, or simply a middle grade.
Philosophers disagree about what makes desert claims reasonable. Possible answers include usefulness, social rules, fitting feelings such as approval, or important values.
Some philosophers think justice means giving people what they deserve. Others question whether desert can explain fair economic and political arrangements.
summaries.why_it_matters: People use words like “deserve” when talking about grades, prizes, punishment, help, respect, wages, and justice. Thinking carefully about desert helps us notice that rules, fairness, effort, need, responsibility, and good results are different considerations. It also helps us ask whether a rule is fair rather than assuming that whatever a rule gives someone is automatically deserved.

important_terms.definition: A judgment that someone should receive a certain benefit, burden, or treatment because of some feature they have or something they did.
A claim that someone should receive something because a rule, law, contract, or other social arrangement gives it to them.
The person, group, or thing said to deserve something.
The thing someone is said to deserve, such as a grade, prize, apology, reward, or punishment.
The feature that is supposed to explain why someone deserves something, such as excellent work or harmful behavior.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone be entitled to something without deserving it? Can someone deserve something without being entitled to it?
What should matter when deciding whether someone deserves a reward: effort, results, need, character, or something else?
Is it fair to punish someone for a bad result if they did not cause it?
Should a society try to give everyone everything they deserve?

summaries.example: Suppose an employee works exceptionally hard and deserves recognition, while another employee has a serious illness caused by circumstances outside their control and deserves care. A simple responsibility view says desert requires responsibility for the desert base, but the second case challenges that principle: the employee may deserve assistance because of harm or need without being responsible for having that condition. The example shows why identifying the desert base is not enough; we must also ask what kind of basis is morally relevant and what treatment expresses it.
summaries.summary: The entry examines desert as a normative relation: a person or other deserver is said to deserve a benefit, burden, attitude, or form of treatment on the basis of some desert base. Familiar cases include grades based on academic work, prizes based on performance, compensation based on injury, and penalties based on wrongdoing. The entry distinguishes this relation from entitlement. Entitlement is tied to social or legal rules, contracts, or institutions; desert does not essentially require such arrangements. Consequently, someone may be entitled to an inheritance while not deserving it, or deserve an opportunity that no rule guarantees. Desert claims can concern persons, groups, and even non-persons, and their objects can be positive, negative, or neutral. The analysis also asks whether desert is basic—perhaps involving approval or disapproval—or derived, with rewards and punishments expressing more fundamental attitudes. Important structural questions concern desert bases, distributors, comparative strength, and timing. Proposed principles include the Aboutness Principle, the Responsibility Principle, and the Temporality Principle, but examples involving innocent victims, illness, compensation, and future wrongdoing create pressure on simple versions of them. The justification of desert claims is equally controversial. Consequentialist accounts appeal to utility, institutional accounts to actual or ideal rules, and appraising-attitude accounts to fitting approval, blame, or related responses. The entry argues that each approach encounters difficulties, including circularity, injustice, and cases where expedient treatment is undeserved. It then considers desert-sensitive theories of intrinsic value, especially theories relating value to welfare and the fit between what:
key_ideas: Desert claims have a structure involving a deserver, a desert, and a desert base; they may also identify a distributor, strength, and relevant times.
Desert and entitlement are structurally similar but conceptually distinct. Entitlement depends essentially on social or legal institutions, whereas desert need not.

Desert bases are contested. Responsibility seems relevant in many cases, but innocent victims, sick children, and people needing care appear to deserve treatment without being responsible for their condition.

Consequentialist justifications identify desert with, or ground it in, beneficial consequences, but the entry argues that utility and desert can come apart: useful punishment may be undeserved, and deserved punishment may reduce welfare.

Institutional accounts face a parallel problem. Actual institutions may be absent or unjust, while ideal institutions risk explaining desert through desert or reproducing consequentialist difficulties.

Desert-sensitive theories of value try to make the fit between people’s welfare and their deserved welfare affect a world’s value. Desertist theories of justice apply the idea to broad or specifically political-economic distributions, but their adequacy remains disputed.
summaries.why_it_matters: Desert language influences judgments about punishment, rewards, compensation, education, employment, and the distribution of social goods. Separating desert from entitlement prevents us from treating existing rules as automatically morally correct. Examining desert bases also reveals how different standards—effort, achievement, responsibility, need, virtue, or contribution—can point in different directions. These distinctions are useful when evaluating claims that a policy, institution, or outcome is just simply because people “got what they deserved.”

important_terms.definition: A normative relation in which a person or other possible deserver is appropriately due some benefit, burden, attitude, or treatment because of a specified basis.
A relation grounded essentially in rules or institutions, such as a legal guarantee or contract, that specifies what someone is to receive.
The person, group, or sometimes non-person that is said to deserve something.
The benefit, burden, attitude, or treatment that is deserved; it may be positive, negative, or neither.
The property or fact in virtue of which a deserver is said to deserve a particular desert.
A proposed requirement that a person must be responsible for possessing the relevant desert base in order to deserve something on that basis.
A proposed requirement that the deserver must already possess the relevant basis when the desert begins, used in discussion of pre-punishment.
A theory holding, in a broad sense, that justice consists in people receiving what they deserve; different versions specify different deserts, bases, and distributors.

questions_to_think_about: Does responsibility have to be necessary for desert, or do compensation, care, and apology provide counterexamples?
Why does the distinction between entitlement and desert matter when an institution is unjust?
Can a treatment be justified because it has good consequences without being deserved?
Should the value of a social outcome depend on how closely welfare matches deserved welfare, and how should that fit be measured?
Can a theory of distributive justice be fundamentally desertist if the institutions that distribute benefits must first be justified by some non-desert consideration?

summaries.example: A school contest has one prize. Maya practiced for months and performed brilliantly, so many people think she deserves the prize. But imagine that the contest rules say the prize goes to the student whose name is drawn from a box. If Jordan’s name is drawn, Jordan may be entitled to the prize under the rules, while Maya may seem to deserve it because of her performance. The example shows why following a rule and receiving what one deserves can come apart.
summaries.summary: Desert is a way of saying that someone should receive something because of a relevant basis. The basis might be excellent work, athletic success, harmful behavior, contribution, effort, need, or being the victim of wrongdoing. A typical claim therefore has a deserver, a desert, and a desert base. It may also identify a distributor, such as a teacher, employer, government, or another person. The entry first separates desert from entitlement. Entitlement depends on rules or institutions: a guarantee can entitle a customer to a refund, and a legal system can entitle an heir to property. Desert need not depend on such rules. Someone may deserve an opportunity, apology, or good fortune even when no institution promises it; conversely, an institution can create an entitlement that seems undeserved. Philosophers also ask whether only people can deserve things, whether deserts must be good or bad, and whether some deserts are basic attitudes such as approval or disapproval while other treatments express those attitudes. Several principles about desert bases are examined. The Aboutness Principle requires the basis to concern the deserver. The Responsibility Principle requires responsibility for the basis, but cases of innocent harm and illness challenge it. The Temporality Principle says the basis must exist when the desert begins, which helps explain objections to punishing someone before a crime, though this too is debated. The entry surveys attempts to justify desert through consequences, institutions, appraising attitudes, or multiple values. key_ideas: A desert claim usually connects a deserver to a desert through a desert base; it may also involve a distributor and the strength or timing of the claim.
Entitlement comes from institutions such as laws, contracts, or school rules. Desert is presented as more purely normative and can exist even when no institution creates a claim.
People may deserve positive, negative, or neutral outcomes. Desert is not limited to rewards, and it is not always a matter of receiving either a benefit or a burden.

Philosophers debate whether responsibility is required. Hard work and wrongdoing fit that idea, but illness, insults, and undeserved harm seem to create claims for care, sympathy, apologies, or compensation.
Consequences and institutions may help explain why some treatment is appropriate, but useful treatment can be undeserved and existing institutions can be unfair.
Justice theories based on desert range from the very broad idea that everyone should receive everything they deserve to narrower views about political and economic benefits supplied by governments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Everyday arguments about fairness often rely on the word “deserve,” but that word can hide several different ideas. A person might have a legal claim, have earned a reward, need compensation, or be responsible for wrongdoing. These are not interchangeable. Studying desert helps us evaluate school rules, workplace decisions, punishment, public benefits, and claims about a just society without assuming that one standard settles every case.

important_terms.definition: The idea that a person should receive a benefit, burden, or treatment because of a relevant feature, action, or condition.
Having a claim recognized by a rule, contract, law, or institution, whether or not the person deserves the result in a moral sense.
The person, group, or sometimes non-person that is said to deserve something.
The thing received or owed in a desert claim, such as a grade, prize, apology, compensation, or penalty.
The feature or fact that is offered as the reason for a desert claim, such as effort, achievement, harm, or wrongdoing.
A person or institution from which the deserver is supposed to receive the desert.
A view that justice is fundamentally about people receiving what they deserve, although versions disagree about what is deserved and why.
A theory saying that the value of an outcome depends partly on how well people’s actual welfare matches the welfare they deserve.

questions_to_think_about: If a rule gives someone a prize, is that enough to show that the person deserves it?
Can someone deserve an apology or medical care even when they did nothing to cause the situation?
Should a person receive punishment for a crime they will commit in the future? Why or why not?
Is an outcome better when people receive exactly the welfare they deserve, even if another outcome creates more total welfare?
What should governments distribute according to desert, if anything?
